title: Who Is Ashoke Sen? The Kolkata Physicist Who Unified String Theory — and Just Became the First Indian to Win the Oskar Klein Medal
excerpt: He did his apprenticeship at Fermilab and Stanford, then chose in 1988 to build his career in India. Four decades later, Ashoke Sen — Breakthrough Prize laureate, Dirac medallist, Fellow of the Royal Society at 42 — has received Stockholm's Oskar Klein Medal, an honour no Indian physicist had won in its 38 years.
body:
• Ashoke Sen, the Kolkata-born theoretical physicist at Bengaluru's International Centre for Theoretical Sciences (ICTS), has been awarded the 2026 Oskar Klein Medal — becoming the first Indian physicist to receive the honour in its 38-year history.
  • Sen delivered the 2026 Oskar Klein Memorial Lecture, "Gravity from Strings and Strings from Gravity," at Stockholm University's AlbaNova Centre on October 22, 2026.
  • His 1994 work on S-duality helped trigger the "second superstring revolution" and earned him a share of the inaugural 2012 Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics; his entropy function formalism let physicists count the microscopic states behind black-hole entropy.
  • Trained at Presidency College, IIT Kanpur and Stony Brook, and seasoned at Fermilab and Stanford, Sen chose in 1988 to build his career in India — a return-home decision, made decades before it was fashionable, that produced world-leading physics from TIFR, the Harish-Chandra Research Institute and now ICTS.

On October 22, 2026, Ashoke Sen stood in Stockholm University's AlbaNova Centre and delivered a lecture titled "Gravity from Strings and Strings from Gravity." With it came the 2026 Oskar Klein Medal, awarded annually by Stockholm University and the Nobel Committee for Physics of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. Sen is the first Indian physicist ever to receive it, according to the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences (ICTS) in Bengaluru, where he holds the ICTS-Infosys Madhava Chair.

The medal, established in 1988 and named for the Swedish theorist Oskar Klein, is not a prize for a single paper. Its first three recipients were Chen-Ning Yang, Steven Weinberg and Hans Bethe — all Nobel laureates. Stephen Hawking received it in 2003, Peter Higgs in 2009 and Kip Thorne in 2016. Sen, 70, now joins that list on the strength of four decades of work that, in the ICTS's words, reflects "pioneering work on S-duality, the precision counting of black-hole entropy and string field theory, all of which have helped shape modern string theory."

"On behalf of all of us, very warm congratulations to Ashoke. It has been no less than wonderful having Ashoke with us and setting the tone for excellence here at ICTS."

— Rajesh Gopakumar, Director, ICTS

A Kolkata education, an American apprenticeship, an Indian career

Sen was born on July 15, 1956, in Kolkata, the elder son of Anil Kumar Sen, a professor of physics at Scottish Church College, and Gouri Sen. He was schooled at Sailendra Sircar Vidyalaya in Kolkata and read physics at Presidency College, where the celebrated relativist Amal Kumar Raychaudhuri was among the teachers who shaped him. He graduated with his BSc in 1975, took a master's degree in physics at IIT Kanpur, and crossed the Atlantic for doctoral work at the State University of New York at Stony Brook, completing his PhD in 1982 under George Sterman.

America gave him the finest apprenticeship theoretical physics offers: postdoctoral years at Fermilab, the United States' premier particle-physics laboratory, from 1982 to 1985, and then at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center until 1988. Then Sen made the decision that defines his biography as much as any equation. At a time when an Indian theorist with Fermilab and Stanford on his CV could have taken his pick of Western chairs, he went home. He joined the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in Mumbai in 1988, moved in the mid-1990s to the Harish-Chandra Research Institute in Allahabad — now Prayagraj — where he spent more than two decades as a distinguished professor, and today holds his chair at ICTS-TIFR in Bengaluru. Visiting appointments followed him rather than the other way round: he is a Morningstar Visiting Professor at MIT and a distinguished professor at the Korea Institute for Advanced Study.

The duality that changed string theory

String theory proposes that the fundamental constituents of nature are not point particles but tiny one-dimensional strings, whose different vibrations appear to us as different particles and forces. Through the 1980s the field had a problem of plenty: several distinct string theories, each internally consistent, with no obvious way to choose between them — and no way to calculate in the regimes where interactions are strong.

Sen's landmark 1994 paper on dyon-monopole bound states and SL(2,Z) invariance provided striking evidence for S-duality: the idea that a string theory at strong coupling — where calculations are intractable — is exactly equivalent to a theory at weak coupling, where they are not. A hard problem in one description became a solvable problem in its mirror. Extended by Sen and others, duality linked the supposedly separate string theories together, and the realisation followed that they were different limits of one underlying theory. Historians of the field call the ferment that followed the second superstring revolution.

That is precisely what the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics honoured in 2012, when Sen was among the nine inaugural laureates, cited "for uncovering striking evidence of strong-weak duality in certain supersymmetric string theories and gauge theories, opening the path to the realization that all string theories are different limits of the same underlying theory." The prize carried $3 million. Characteristically, the work continued exactly as before — chalk, blackboard, and the next problem.

"For me, the best part of doing science is that I can work on whatever interests me most."

— Ashoke Sen, Breakthrough Prize laureate profile

Counting what is inside a black hole

Sen's second great programme attacked one of physics' deepest puzzles. Since the 1970s, the Bekenstein-Hawking formula has assigned black holes an entropy — a measure of hidden microscopic states — without anyone being able to count those states directly. The difficulty was structural: the counting can be done where gravity is weak, but black holes exist only where it is strong.

Sen's entropy function formalism cut through that impasse. As the Infosys Prize jury put it when it honoured him in Mathematical Sciences in 2009, the formalism "made it possible to link Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of black holes to the degeneracy count of states in the corresponding String Theory," resolving for the first time a problem that had blocked the field. His precision counting of black-hole microstates — extended since to the quantum corrections beyond the Bekenstein-Hawking value — remains one of the sharpest tests any theory of quantum gravity has passed, and the programme is still being pursued.

Around those two pillars sits a body of work few theorists can match for range: he pioneered the study of unstable D-branes and framed the Sen conjecture on open-string tachyon condensation; his account of rolling tachyons fed into string cosmology; and he has co-authored foundational papers on string field theory, the attempt to give strings the same rigorous field-theoretic footing as particles. The through-line is a preference for exact answers in a field often forced to settle for approximations.

An honours list four decades long

The Oskar Klein Medal is the latest entry in a list that began early. Sen won the ICTP Prize in 1989 and India's Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize in 1994. In 1998, aged 42, he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in London — nominated, the Infosys Prize records, by Stephen Hawking. The G.D. Birla Award (1996) and the TWAS Prize (1997) sit alongside fellowships of all three Indian science academies. India decorated him with the Padma Shri in 2001 and the Padma Bhushan in 2013. The Breakthrough Prize came in 2012 and the ICTP's Dirac Medal — theoretical physics' other great honour, shared that year for contributions to the origin and development of string theory — in 2014. We profiled a fellow Dirac medallist, the statistical physicist Deepak Dhar, in this series: Who Is Deepak Dhar?

What distinguishes Sen's list is where the honoured work was done. Almost all of it — the duality papers, the entropy formalism, the tachyon work — was produced at Indian institutions, on Indian salaries, with Indian students. The medals kept arriving in Stockholm, London and Trieste; the return address stayed in Mumbai, Prayagraj and Bengaluru.

Why he matters to the diaspora

For Indian scientists abroad weighing the familiar equation — stay for the laboratories and the funding, or return for the life and the purpose — Sen is the existence proof that the second path does not cap the first ambition. He left India fully trained, absorbed everything Fermilab and Stanford could teach, and then spent 38 years demonstrating that foundational physics of the very first rank can be done from India, provided the thinker is willing to be patient and the institutions are willing to protect the thinking. The generations of Indian string theorists who trained around TIFR, HRI and ICTS are the multiplier on that choice.

At 70, holding a named chair at the institute whose director says he sets "the tone for excellence," Sen is still working the same seam his Stockholm lecture described: how gravity emerges from strings, and what strings reveal about gravity. The Oskar Klein Medal does not close that story. By the standards of his career — one breakthrough per decade, each built to last — it reads more like a progress report.

items.event: Ashoke Sen is born in Kolkata.
BSc in physics from Presidency College, Kolkata.
PhD from Stony Brook University; begins postdoctoral work at Fermilab.
Returns to India to join the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Mumbai.
Landmark S-duality paper helps trigger the second superstring revolution; wins the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize.
Elected Fellow of the Royal Society at age 42.
Among the nine inaugural Breakthrough Prize laureates in Fundamental Physics.
Awarded the Dirac Medal by the ICTP.
Delivers the Oskar Klein Memorial Lecture in Stockholm and receives the 2026 Oskar Klein Medal — the first Indian physicist to do so.
